posts.excerpt: Sections: The test | What came back | How we checked it | What it cost | About Qwen4 Max | Run it on Together AI | FAQs | How much does Qwen4 Max cost on Together AI? We gave Qwen4 Max a bug report and an entire codebase in one request. The codebase was Tornado, the Python web framework: all 344 files, 652,519 tokens. The model had no tools, and we didn't select relevant files or run a retrieval step first. Seventy-two seconds later it returned a patch, and the patch passes the tests Tornado's maintainers wrote for that bug. The request cost 69 cents. It also found a precedent elsewhere in the repository. The bug report never mentions tornado/iostream.py , but the model pointed to code there that already handles errors the way its patch needed to. Tornado's maintainers cite the same code in their own fix. Qwen4 Max is Alibaba's flagship Qwen model. It's live on Together AI today, and it's 30% off through November 22, 2026. Tornado is an open-source Python web framework. Its repository holds about 340 files of code, tests and docs. That fits in Qwen4 Max's context window, and it's far more than anyone would paste into a prompt by hand. We picked a fix the maintainers committed on November 18, 2026, two days after Qwen4 Max was released, and tested against the repository as it was just before that commit. This is one example, chosen to show what a single call can do and what it costs. The bug is in Tornado's websocket code. When a connection closed with messages still unsent, every write_message() call that wasn't awaited logged an error, even though awaiting it is optional…

posts.title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
posts.summary: ruby2shell lets attackers corrupt memory in default Rails and Sinatra apps without logging in. Cloudflare WAF blocks it for every customer, including Free plans. Upgrade Ruby now, and use the WAF to cover the gap.
posts.excerpt: Sections: What we know about ruby2shell | Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposed | Who is affected | Six more Ruby flaws in the same release | How Cloudflare WAF protects you | New managed rules, on for every customer | What the WAF cannot see | Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell ( CVE-2026-132825 ), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 . The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure. Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases. The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. posts.title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
posts.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | The Loop | Serving the Loop in vLLM | Variable-Loop Research Checkpoint | Accuracy Evals Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. The best way to cut costs and speed up your agents has always been hidden in plain sight. Building harnesses have evolved from a discipline of addition to one of subtraction as we move into a world of lean, bitter-lesson-pilled harnesses. Edge cases and guardrails that used to contextualize the model for a task are now more often than not bloat. So how do we let the model's judgment and intelligence shine through? One way to do this in practice is to retrieve tools just in time on a per-task basis, instead of preloading them, called deferred tool loading. posts.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
posts.summary: On November 3, 2026 U.S. voters headed to the polls. Here’s what Cloudflare data across more than 1,400 protected sites tells us about Election Day Internet traffic and cyberattacks.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks | Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle | PHP vulnerability | Recommendations Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026. Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States. These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year. posts.title: Optimizing DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash PD & Colocate Serving on H20-3e
posts.summary: We optimized disaggregated DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash serving on H20-3e by tuning prefill and decode parallelism, supporting BCG with prefill CP and bounded SWA replay, and speeding up Indexer kernels.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Overview | Measurement Setup | 1. Prefill CP and Decode DP | 2. FP8 DeepGEMM for the Prefill Indexer | 3. Breakable CUDA Graphs for Prefill | 4. Tensor-Parallel MoE | 5. Larger Indexer Score Tiles | 6. Fuse Prefill Selection and Writeback We optimized disaggregated DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash serving on H20-3e by tuning prefill and decode parallelism, supporting BCG with prefill CP and bounded SWA replay, and speeding up Indexer kernels. Compared with TP4, the final configuration cut mean end-to-end latency by 65.5% and delivered 2.91× the output throughput. Our intra-node PD deployment used four GPUs each for prefill and decode, with KV cache transfers over NVLink. Mean end-to-end latency fell from 13.63 s to 4.70 s , and output throughput rose from 847 to 2,465 tokens/s . Prefill context parallelism paired with decode data parallelism gave the largest gain, followed by FP8 DeepGEMM scoring. Most of the latency gain came before the first token. Mean time to first token (TTFT) fell from 12.04 s to 1.89 s. Mean time per output token after the first (TPOT) rose from 3.20 to 5.62 ms. At fixed concurrency, faster prefill can keep decode busier, and faster decode can free client slots for new prompts. That can shift queueing between the two workers. In the original sweep, the median prefill queue fell from 15 requests at baseline to 9 after CP and DP, then to 4 after DeepGEMM and 3 after breakable graphs. It reached zero with TP MoE. The median decode queue stayed at zero. The router sends each request through prefill and decode. The workers transfer the KV state directly…

posts.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
posts.summary: Java4Shell is a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that can lead to remote code execution. Cloudflare has released six WAF managed rules for paid plans that logs matching requests by default. Patch your Java runtimes now.
posts.excerpt: Sections: What we know about the vulnerability | Who is affected | Mitigate if you cannot patch right away | Protect your infrastructure while you patch | New managed rules | Adding defense-in-depth with WAF attack score | Deploy protections and patch | Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) , a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC. The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed , and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. posts.title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
posts.summary: Every agent turn resends the full session. Together AI and Ollama break down how to protect the prefix cache, from the harness to the GPU.
posts.excerpt: Sections: What an agent turn looks like to a GPU | Cache is king | The harnesses and APIs | Loading tools late | Things at the top that change | Reasoning effort | Big tool results | Subagents Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps. Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more. This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. posts.summary: Training large language models involves calculating and storing a lot of numbers. Using fewer bits for each value reduces memory usage and allows GPUs to perform calculations faster. posts.excerpt: Sections: Choosing a target for quantization | Low-precision formats on Blackwell | Block-scaled backward passes | Re-quantization with stochastic rounding | Quantized communications | Kernels for low-precision training | Recipe details | Closing thoughts Training large language models involves calculating and storing a lot of numbers. Using fewer bits for each value reduces memory usage and allows GPUs to perform calculations faster. However, there is a tradeoff: fewer bits also mean fewer representable numbers, leading to more aggressive rounding. Lower-precision representations ultimately hurt accuracy by adding error to the calculations. For example, suppose we want to store the number 3.2, but the nearest values our numerical format can represent are 3 and 4. Rounding to 3 introduces a quantization error of − 0.2 , the difference between the actual value and the one that can be represented in the quantized format. A single error like this may seem small, but these errors accumulate over training as rounding happens repeatedly across layers and optimization steps, which can impair the learning process. This is the central challenge of low-precision training: how can we benefit from faster arithmetic without introducing errors that interfere with learning? We manage this tradeoff through our use of three key numerical formats during training: BF16, MXFP8, and NVFP4. Each format’s precision is fixed, but its speed depends on the hardware being used. posts.excerpt: Sections: What it looks like on Modal: active-resource pricing | Estimating Sandbox costs on Modal | Why bursting works | How should I size my Modal Sandboxes? | Minimizing the impact of evictions | Summary Across Modal, a typical Sandbox spends more than half its life using less than 6% of its peak CPU. Take a coding agent: the Sandbox sits nearly idle while the model reasons about what to do next, and spikes only when the agent installs dependencies, runs tests, or builds the project. The same pattern shows up in other common Sandbox workloads: RL rollouts, evals, and app builders. Today, most sandboxes are priced based on a fixed-resource reservation model. Reservations are a poor fit for spiky work, for two reasons: We believe your bill should align with your workload, rising when it’s busy and falling when it’s idle. That’s why our Sandboxes burst: a Sandbox gets the CPU and memory it needs when your work spikes and gives them back when it is done. You pay for what you actually use. Every Sandbox bursts by default. Start with the base 0.125 cores and 128 MiB request and let your Sandbox grow as it needs. With active-resource pricing, you pay each second for what you use, with the small request as a floor. You can request more to guarantee it, but you’ll pay for those resources even when your Sandbox is idle. You can also set a limit to cap how far your Sandbox can burst; think of it as setting the size of the computer the Sandbox lives on. posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | Introduction | Our Approach: Decide the Config at Compile Time | How the Heuristics Work | Result 1: Config Quality, with No Tuning Time | Linear attention | vLLM’s reduction kernels | The everyday kernels, against torch.compile Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and chooses block sizes, warps, and stages, giving near-autotuned speed for free. Helion, PyTorch’s domain-specific language (DSL) for performance portable machine learning kernels, relies heavily on autotuning for its performance. Autotuning time can be a major bottleneck: for example, a previous team tuning a single paged-attention kernel across 72 shapes spent 10 hours in Helion’s quick mode, and 25 at full effort. To address these issues, we’ve developed a set of heuristics that read a kernel’s IR and dataflow at compile time and emit a config directly, without any autotuning . We classify kernels into broad families based on the operations they contain – matmul, reduction, or pointwise – and apply a family-specific heuristic to each. These families are intentionally general: the matmul heuristic, for example, looks for any kernel containing a matmul operation such as hl.dot or torch.baddbmm, not just standard m-n-k matrix multiplications. These are designed to be generic and apply broadly to custom kernels that users may write. A single Helion kernel can lower into thousands of different Triton kernels. posts.excerpt: Sections: Why a small model matters for research | The research challenge | Why co-design mattered | Benchmark methodology and dataset | Optimizing on Google Cloud TPU v7 | Phase I: align basic workload configuration to establish a proper baseline | Phase II: cross-stack decode co-design, from MaxText and vLLM down to XLA and Pallas | Phase III: optimize the whole RL cycle Generative reasoning is reshaping how ranking and decision systems work. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [ arXiv:2606.31984 ] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability? A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time. Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination. We ran RL for a 0.6-billion-parameter model on a 64-chip Google Cloud TPU v7 (Ironwood) slice. The model has far fewer weights than the large dense and mixture-of-experts systems that usually motivate…

posts.title: SGLang-Neuron v0.1.0: SGLang's Serving Stack on AWS Trainium
posts.summary: Today we are releasing SGLang-Neuron v0.1.0, the first public release of SGLang's backend for AWS Trainium. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers the best economics for AI training and inference at scale. It follows the closed beta the SGLang team announced in October.
posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | Introduction | How it works | One asynchronous runtime | Megakernels: one kernel per step | Prefill-decode disaggregation over EFA | Kimi-K3 on three Trainium3 nodes | GLM-5.2 at 1M context Today we are releasing SGLang-Neuron v0.1.0, the first public release of SGLang’s backend for AWS Trainium . Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers the best economics for AI training and inference at scale. It follows the closed beta the SGLang team announced in October. The beta showed that SGLang’s model components carry over to Trainium through TorchNeuron . This release is about what it takes to make them fast. Neuron compiles models into programs that run on Trainium’s NeuronCores , work reaches those cores through launch queues, and the fastest code paths are hand-written NKI kernels. Most of the engineering in v0.1.0 went into three places where that matters: how steps are launched, how much of a step lives in one kernel, and where the KV cache sits when it is not on the device. This blog covers what ships in v0.1.0 and where it goes next. We start with how the backend is built: the plugin architecture, the asynchronous runtime, megakernels, prefill-decode disaggregation over EFA, HiCache, and SGLang Diffusion on Neuron. We then cover the supported features and models, RL rollouts with Miles, how to get started, and the roadmap. SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin. Installing it registers a neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry point, and SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron selects it at launch. Figure 1: How the SGLang-Neuron plugin fits into…

posts.excerpt: Sections: 01 · A Primer on Robotics | How the JEPA architecture fills the "plan" box | Where the sixteen seconds actually goes | 02 · The Approach | 03 · A Primer on Ray | A general framework for turning Python into a cluster program | Ray Core | Ray Serve With V-JEPA2-AC the system decides what a robot arm should do next by assessing hundreds of possible futures and picking the one closest to the goal. It takes a significant amount of time between moves. This document presents a design and tested implementation for getting that under a second by moving the search into a Ray cluster. A robot perceives a partial observation of the environment, selects an action via some policy, executes it through a controller, and repeats this at control-loop frequency. Classically, each of those three functions is solved in closed form, and a CPU on the robot is enough to run all of them. Classical robotics built each of those three boxes from first principles: hand-derived kinematics for perception, trajectory optimization for planning, PID or model-predictive controllers for control. This approach, depicted in Figure 1, underlies decades of industrial automation, but every new task, object, or environment typically requires new engineering. Physical AI aims to replace some or all of those boxes with networks trained on data, trading hand-derived precision for generality: a model trained on sufficient data transfers to situations not explicitly programmed for. posts.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
posts.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | Model Architecture | vLLM Integration & Optimization | Performance | Accuracy Evals vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships…

posts.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
posts.summary: Cloudflare is building an experimental consensus service using a never-before-deployed consensus algorithm, QuePaxa. In this post we explain how QuePaxa works and why we chose it.
posts.excerpt: Sections: What we’re building and why it’s unique | The challenges of consensus at a global scale | Destructive interference and leaders | When leader recovery is unstable | When fault detection goes awry | When fault detection is slow | Why QuePaxa is the right fit | How QuePaxa works under the hood Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. Meerkat is a…

posts.title: Unified Memory in SGLang: One Arena for Every Token Lifetime
posts.summary: Attention layers need their past to compute the next token, but not every layer remembers it the same way:
posts.excerpt: Sections: Hybrid models and the memory split | A new KV layout: one entry per token | One arena, different allocation geometries | Composing all three state types | Request-scoped state | Admission: can the whole request fit? | Keeping pages safe during in-flight work | One memory system, three interfaces Attention layers need their past to compute the next token, but not every layer remembers it the same way: GPT-OSS and Muse Spark interleave full and sliding-window attention. Qwen3.5 interleaves full attention with linear-attention layers. Kimi K3 pairs KDA linear attention with MLA, and K3.1 replaces the MLA layers with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). Their demands do not scale together. A long-context workload grows full-attention KV; many short concurrent requests need more window KV and state slots even though each request’s history is small. The pressure can shift within one request, too: its state slots are taken when it starts, while its full-attention KV keeps growing. SGLang’s default design gives each kind of state its own pool, a sub-pool , and fixes their sizes at startup through --swa-full-tokens-ratio and --mamba-full-memory-ratio . The right ratio depends on traffic you do not know yet. A long-context workload can exhaust the full-attention pool while much of the pool for the bounded states (window KV and recurrent state) sits idle, and many short requests do the reverse. The free bytes exist, but the other pool is not allowed to use them. Choosing the ratio well means profiling your workload, and when the traffic changes, memory is stranded behind… In…

Browser inference ensures privacy by keeping users’ prompts, model inputs, and outputs on the user’s device rather than the server. This reduces network latency, enables offline use-cases, and lowers server-side inference costs. With the ExecuTorch WebGPU backend, PyTorch models get a native path to GPU-accelerated inference in WebGPU-enabled browsers on desktop, laptop and mobile. WebGPU, the modern successor to WebGL, provides native compute shaders, shared memory, storage buffers, and barriers, making it viable for high-performance ML inference directly in the browser. Today, running a PyTorch model in the browser usually means first converting it to another framework’s format, such as GGUF, ONNX or TFLite. The ExecuTorch WebGPU backend lets PyTorch models reach the browser without leaving the PyTorch toolchain. posts.title: The Scale-Up Memory Tier
posts.summary: Long-context inference puts pressure on GPU HBM memory. As context grows, KV caches take up more space, competing with model weights and other data for HBM capacity.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Workloads | Shared KV cache | Active KV cache for sparse attention | Embedding tables for recommendation models | Engram tables | RL rollouts for post-training Long-context inference puts pressure on GPU HBM memory. As context grows, KV caches take up more space, competing with model weights and other data for HBM capacity. Netpreme’s scale-up memory tier provides a pooled DRAM layer for this data. The G1–G4 labels follow the terminology used in NVIDIA’s CMX memory hierarchy . Figure 1 shows Netpreme’s adaptation of this hierarchy: GPUs reach memory and storage through different access paths. They access HBM and compatible system memory through memory operations; the G3 tier shown here uses block I/O over the scale-out network. From G3 down, every access pays the block I/O tax — microseconds of protocol and queuing latency per transfer. The G2 scale-up memory tier operates with native memory semantics, keeping access latencies orders of magnitude lower. The scale-up memory tier sits between HBM and storage. It pools DRAM across the rack on the scale-up fabric, with load/store access on compatible accelerator and fabric configurations. What next? For multi-gigabyte AI images, most pull time goes to unpacking gzip layers, not the network. We benchmarked zstd on Crusoe Managed Kubernetes: 2.4–3.0× faster cold pulls, 2.2–2.4× faster pod startup, and 4.4× faster on a 13 GB image with containerd parallel unpack. Pulling a 3.6 GB NVIDIA CUDA® image from a registry in the same region took 51.5 seconds. Pulling it from NVIDIA's public registry over the internet took 56.2 seconds. Moving the registry next door saved 8%. The bottleneck was gzip. Converting that image to zstd cut the pull to 17.4 seconds. On a 24.3 GB NVIDIA NeMo™ image the same change saved 4 minutes per node. On an 8-GPU node, that is 32 GPU-minutes of idle accelerators every cold start. A pull has three phases: resolve the manifest, download the compressed layers, and unpack them, which means decompressing each layer and writing it to disk. Download and unpack overlap, and unpack is the long pole. In our measurements on 7 GB and 13 GB images, unpack accounted for about 80% of total pull time, and containerd unpacks layers one at a time by default. Many public container images are compressed with gzip, a format from the early 1990s, and decompressing them is what makes unpack slow. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. posts.summary: Together GPU Clusters auto repair detects GPU, host and fabric faults, picks the lightest fix, and lets you decide per fault and per Xid code which repairs run automatically. Here is how it works.

Bring your own detector | 4. Repair actions and the escalation ladder | 5. Rails that assume the alert storm will happen | 6. The machine re-validates itself At cluster scale, GPU faults are a reality. An Xid error, a double-bit ECC error, a GPU falling off the PCIe bus or a flapping InfiniBand link can stall a distributed training job or take an inference replica down. Spotting that something is wrong is usually the easy part. The hard part is everything between the fault and a healthy node again Earlier this year, we announced the launch of our fully Automatic node remediation features. Our GPU clusters customers and our internal Inference platform has been using this capability to help drive workload resiliency and minimize down time. Our customers love this capability, and we wanted to take some time break the system down and explain how it works and why we designed it this way. posts.excerpt: Sections: Agents made inference a memory problem | HBM cannot hold every agent’s state | Outcomes set the score | The missing tier sits at the rack | Panel discussion summary On October 14, 2026, Netpreme hosted the panel “Cracking the Memory Wall for Next-Gen AI Infrastructure” near the OCP Global Summit with a group of industry leaders: The panel agreed on the problem in the first five minutes. Agents have made inference a memory problem. The rest of the hour was about where the memory, and the state in it, should live. Sudeep Bhoja founded d-Matrix in 2019, when CNNs set the agenda. He traced the shift in one line. “CNNs was a compute-bound problem…ever since autoregressive decoding in GPT-2 it became a memory-bound problem.” Angela Yeung of Cerebras tied the next step to agents. Context per request keeps growing, and agents reuse the same context across many queries. “Your agent is only useful if it actually has information about you, right? All the information about you is not going to fit into 100K of context.” That context, she said, “has to be stored somewhere easily accessible, whether that’s on the accelerator or in close access to the accelerator.” Weights stay in the fastest tier because every token touches them. KV cache for a million-token context is still large after years of compression work. When an agent pauses for a tool call, that state sits idle in the most expensive memory in the system. “If you go for a tool call and spend thirty seconds, it doesn’t make a lot of sense to keep all of that state on the HBM tier, and this is where memory tiering is…

TL;DR: In The 4-bitter Lesson , we showed how to use the high throughput of NVFP4 Tensor Cores for stable RL. This time, we show it is possible to improve the speed and accuracy of the most optimized NVFP4 kernels in the memory-bound decode phase by actually increasing their precision, pushing NVFP4 beyond its widely assumed limits for both inference serving and RL rollouts. Low-precision inference usually comes with a tradeoff: faster execution for larger numerical errors. Four-bit weights and activations would appear to be the fastest possible option, while higher precision means sacrificing speed. The benefits of low precision come from both the decreased memory traffic from low precision data and higher hardware throughput for low precision computation. In the decode phase, data traffic dominates while arithmetic capacity sits idle. Therefore, four bit storage is valuable while four bit computation offers no speed advantage. Thus, we keep weights in NVFP4 but let activations stay in BF16. This keeps almost all the memory traffic benefits of having both in NVFP4. That changes how the tool and the dies move: each die rides its own holder past the process stations, and the tools get closer at each station to process the dies. The track’s independent shuttles also lift station utilization, save on duplicate tooling, and enable heterogeneous integration. We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for Hybrid Bonding. These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography. Despite the advantages, ASML still needs to solve challenges around feed-forward metrology, the die-to-wafer contact, the modification of the non-bonding tools so they can process dies on the track, and keeping the whole loop clean. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is built for customization and deployment in specialized enterprise workflows. Within the Nemotron 3 family of models, it serves as the high-accuracy multimodal execution model, complementing Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Nemotron 3 Ultra. posts.title: SGLang and Miles Add Day-0 Support for Muse Spark Open
posts.summary: Muse Spark Open combines a sparse language decoder with visual and audio encoders, bringing multimodal inputs into a shared token-generation pipeline.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Highlights | Muse Spark Open Architecture | GQA and Sliding-Window Attention | Text, Audio, Images and Video | MoE with Pooler, Unpooler and Per-Expert Normalization | Feature Support | Runtime Optimization | Kernel Optimizations Muse Spark Open combines a sparse language decoder with visual and audio encoders, bringing multimodal inputs into a shared token-generation pipeline. Multimodal encoders feed a shared language decoder. The expanded MoE block shows feature-width compression and per-expert normalization before aggregation. For its 1M-token context window, Muse Spark Open combines grouped-query attention (GQA) with a hybrid of sliding-window and global attention . GQA shares key/value heads among groups of query heads, reducing the KV-cache footprint. Sliding-window layers attend to a bounded recent context, while periodic global layers retain access to the full sequence. This balances local attention efficiency with long-range information flow, without requiring every layer to maintain full-context attention. Muse Spark Open processes text, audio, images and video as inputs to its language decoder. Images and video frames share a NaViT visual encoder, while waveform audio passes through a dedicated audio encoder. Their outputs are projected into the decoder’s hidden dimension and placed alongside text embeddings, allowing the language model to generate responses grounded in multiple modalities. The MoE block surrounds its routed SwiGLU experts with learned pooler and unpooler projections . The pooler compresses each token’s hidden vector from the model…

posts.title: Push-Based KV Transfer to Improve TTFT and TPOT for Disaggregated Inference in vLLM
posts.summary: A push-based NIXL connector for vLLM disaggregated serving: the prefill instance writes KV directly into decode memory over RDMA, taking the router relay, decode-side allocation, and transfer setup off the TTFT critical path.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Push-based KV transfer | Architecture overview | Implementation details | Threading model | Timing comparison: Pull vs push | Performance data | How to run benchmark | Conclusion vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires… One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over RDMA-capable interconnects such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA, enabling NIXL to transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the… This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. posts.title: Adaptive Verification Without a Confidence Head
posts.summary: An online-fitted acceptance estimator that lets every draft-model speculator use Adaptive Verification, by predicting the target's acceptance probability from the drafter's own logits and refitting continuously during serving.
posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | Background | Problem | Prior Work | Solution: Online-Fitted Acceptance Estimator | Scoring the Distribution | Fitting the Coefficients | Benchmarks Confidence scoring is now supported for all draft-model-based speculator types. In the absence of a confidence head, an online-fitted estimator derives a feature from the drafter's logits to predict the target model's probability of accepting it, which is used directly as a confidence score for Adaptive Verification. The estimator's coefficients are continuously fitted, adapting to the incoming data traffic. This feature landed in PR #52228 , and is enabled with enable_adaptive_verification for draft models without a confidence head. vLLM's Adaptive Verification (AV) enables verification of a subset of the drafted tokens during speculative decoding. Draft tokens with low probability of acceptance are trimmed from the batch before running the target model's forward pass, saving on compute. This optimization is particularly beneficial while serving large batch sizes, because in that regime the GPU becomes compute-bound. See this vLLM blog post for more details. AV needs a per-token estimate of acceptance probability, which is why, until now, it only supported DSpark drafters. DSpark models often ship with a confidence head: a small linear layer over the drafter's hidden state for each position, trained as a binary classifier for "will the target accept this token?" Draft models that lack a confidence head, such as EAGLE, MTP, DFlash, and some DSpark checkpoints, miss out on AV entirely. To use it, these drafters…

posts.excerpt: Sections: What is KubeRay | Before and after KubeRay | Where KubeRay fits between Ray and Kubernetes | What KubeRay provides | Key features | How to deploy KubeRay | Join the Ray community Ray is an open-source framework for scaling Python and AI workloads across many machines. It handles everything from distributed training to online serving through a single Python API, so users can write code once and run it on a laptop or a thousand-node cluster. Kubernetes, on the other hand, is where most organizations already run their infrastructure. GPUs, quotas, access control, networking, and monitoring are all managed there. Teams that adopt Ray rarely want a second cluster manager alongside Kubernetes. They want Ray to run on the Kubernetes they already have. The challenge is that Kubernetes only understands its own native resources like Pods, Services, and Jobs. It has no concept of a Ray cluster, a Ray job, or a Ray Serve application. Running Ray directly on Kubernetes therefore means writing your own glue: Deployments for the head and workers, a Service for the head, scripts to submit jobs and wait for them, and custom logic to scale workers or recover from failures. Every team ends up rebuilding the same plumbing. KubeRay closes this gap. It is an open-source Kubernetes operator that brings Ray into the Kubernetes ecosystem, providing Kubernetes-native lifecycle management, autoscaling, scheduling, reliability, and observability for Ray workloads. KubeRay is the standard way to run Ray on Kubernetes today, and is the foundation of the managed Ray offerings from major cloud…

posts.title: Toward RL on mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers
posts.summary: We trained a model on agentic coding tasks using fully asynchronous RL and mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers. With off-policy correction, training stayed stable through convergence, on par with homogeneous samplers, at a lower cost.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Our setup | Making mixed-sampler RL stable | On par with homogeneous samplers at lower cost | Where training–inference mismatch comes from | Why not true on-policy RL? | How off-policy correction works | What our runs show | Limitations In large-model reinforcement learning (RL), samplers usually run on the same accelerators and often the same precision as the trainer, keeping the two numerically close for stable training. Outside of RL, however, serving systems are not constrained in this manner: they’re free to optimize generation for speed and cost using low-precision formats such as FP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4, co-designed kernels, and even accelerators built just for long-context prefill. Since sampling already takes 80 – 85 % of the GPUs in large RL runs, this leaves a lot on the table! We ask whether we can use mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers , each running its own kernels, while keeping training stable and performant. The first problem is learning. Each of these optimizations adds to training–inference mismatch, making samples more off-policy, which often destabilizes training. Off-policy correction is the natural solution; it lets a trainer learn from data generated by a different policy, such as stale samples in asynchronous training. Since it makes no assumption about why the two policies differ, it should apply equally to different precisions or accelerators. The second problem is the system. RL infrastructure is usually built around clusters of homogeneous accelerators. Mixed samplers require the opposite: autoscaling accelerators that burst…

posts.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
posts.summary: As our merges per day grew more than tenfold, source control became our biggest development bottleneck. Here, we share how we migrated to an in-house version control system in five months.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Growing our monorepo | Principles for agent-scale source control | How Scion works | What we learned building Scion | Contributing to the wider ecosystem | Authors & acknowledgements Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion. At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how…

posts.title: Improve TTFT for Multi-Turn Agentic Workloads with Bi-Directional KV Transfer in vLLM
posts.summary: Bi-directional KV transfer lets vLLM prefill nodes reuse previously computed KV from decode nodes on later conversation turns, cutting redundant prefill recompute and reducing TTFT by up to 3.3x on long multi-turn prompts.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Bi-directional KV transfer | NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer | KV-cache-aware router | Block retention TTL | KV recompute threshold | Performance data | Qwen3-32B | zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its KV cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes do not, increasing the probability of cache… For customers building conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. posts.title: Cut coding agent costs by 90%: Secure LLM serving with Ray + vLLM on Anyscale
posts.summary: Serve coding agents on your own GPUs. A guide to Ray Serve and vLLM on Anyscale, from engine tuning to cache-aware routing, with measured results.
posts.excerpt: Sections: How coding agents shift the serving workload | Coding agents produce far more than chat traffic | Ray Serve LLM scales it for production | Deploy an LLM for coding agents | Step 1: Select an LLM for task success, not leaderboard rank alone | Step 2: Fit weights, runtime memory, and KV cache to the hardware | Step 3: Configure the engine for the model and workload | Step 4: Enable direct streaming and connect the clients Coding agents repeatedly send repository context, instructions, tool results, and conversation history to generate actions. That work is also some of the most sensitive you do: your source, your internal docs, your architecture decisions, leaving your perimeter on every keystroke. posts.excerpt: Sections: Optimizations | TileRT | Lightning Indexer | Sparse MLA | MLA Modifications | IndexShare | Pipeline | RL Training Algorithm How does sparse attention affect the TAM of memory, including HBM and NAND? Sparse attention selects top-k most relevant tokens to attend to, reducing the memory consumption and bandwidth requirements during the core Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA) operation. However, the efficiency improvement doesn’t directly translate to overall memory savings in practice . Concretely, the top-k selection operation typically requires the full context to be in HBM, so sparse attention doesn’t eliminate the memory capacity bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, the SGLang team designed HiSparse, a hierarchical memory system that proactively offloads KV cache entries from device HBM to host DRAM. HiSparse behaves like an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache , where it loads tokens from DRAM to HBM upon top-k selection cache miss, and it offloads tokens from HBM to DRAM based on the LRU eviction policy. To reduce the cache miss latency, HiSparse overlaps KV cache loading of layer N with the execution of layer N-1 (layer-wise overlapping), introduced in HiSparse’s prior work HiCache. With HiSparse, SGLang greatly boosts throughput at high concurrency and long context scenarios, at the cost of top-k cache miss I/O overhead. Sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth requirements at the SDPA operation, but it does not reduce the overall memory capacity usage. Before it can act, it needs to choose. A JEV-like decision model can return a category or score instead of a prose explanation. Application code uses that signal to act. Efficient serving starts with two choices: what information each judgment should see and how to return the scores the application needs . In this post, we explain pointwise and setwise prompts, use Open-Jev’s candidate evaluations as a concrete example, and show where SGLang’s Score API and shared-context execution improve pointwise serving. In our example, the inputs are the current state, a question, and the available actions. Selecting a category is classification. Assigning suitability scores to actions is scoring; those scores can drive selection or ranking. This abstraction describes a serving workload, not the internals of a proprietary JEV model. posts.title: Watermarking in vLLM
posts.summary: How vLLM implements distribution-preserving Gumbel-max text watermarking with efficient GPU kernels, statistical detection, speculative decoding, and repeated-context safeguards.
posts.excerpt: Sections: What is text provenance, and why is it challenging? | Non-distortion | Robustness | Speed | Minimal detection dependencies | Exploiting randomness in LLMs | Gumbel-max Trick | Detecting a watermark Establishing the provenance of digital content is essential to build trust and accountability in the information we share. Watermarking offers a solution: it alters a work to embed a message about it [1] , for instance its provenance. Images and audio can embed watermarks as a subtle perturbation, but these techniques are not applicable to text due to its discrete nature. Instead of trying to perturb the text itself, we influence the generation process in a way that is detectable but does not modify the expected output distribution. Watermarking text is both a scientific and engineering challenge, and there are several requirements that we must aim to balance to have a practical solution: Adding a watermark should not modify the expected output distribution of a model [2] : it should not systematically favour certain words, writing styles, or solutions to problems. Generated text can be altered in many ways: shortened, edited, mixed with other corpora, or even rephrased by another LLM. A good watermarking system aims to preserve its provenance signal even under such modification. Watermarking should add minimal latency and memory overhead to generation and detection. This is particularly important in a high-throughput serving engine such as vLLM. posts.title: Every byte counts: ARCv3 and the case for cross-region RL
posts.summary: Fireworks’ ARCv3 delivers lossless BF16 weight updates nearly 50% smaller than ARCv2, making cross-region reinforcement learning more practical.
posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | Inside ARCv3: Not all updates are created equal | How ARCv3 compares to the field | Using ARCv3 | Making distributed compute work for RL As more teams push into reinforcement learning to train their own frontier-scale models, two things matter more than ever: getting access to training compute, and optimizing the pipes that move data between the machines doing that training. RL is uniquely demanding on those pipes. A frontier model can have trillions of parameters, and the trainer needs to keep pushing updated versions of it out to a fleet of machines generating rollouts, continuously, as training progresses. When those pipes can’t keep up, teams get pushed toward a single option: one massive co-located cluster with everything wired together on the same physical floor. That’s expensive, hard to get, and locks smaller players out. At Fireworks, we take every available path to keep that from being the only option. Otherwise, we end up with a training market only a handful of companies can enter. In a previous post, Frontier RL is cheaper than you think , we walked through how we make cross-region RL work in practice. The core observation is that, in the RL workloads we examined, only about 2% of the model’s BF16 weights changed between consecutive checkpoints. So instead of shipping the full 1 TB checkpoint to every rollout machine every time the trainer takes a step, we ship a compact delta, a compressed description of what changed, and reconstruct the updated model on the other end. That’s what keeps a training run in sync across three or four regions…

Health checks always run before traffic moves; on a canary you can also add metric gates (say p95 latency or error rate) that run after each step. If a gate trips, the rollout pauses at the canary share and you cancel it and run it in reverse. Below we run one for real: a Qwen2.5-7B → Qwen3.5-9B canary whose gate caught a 137% p95 regression at 10% of traffic; we canceled and reversed it with live requests served and none failed. If you run a model in production, you already know the need to swap in a new checkpoint or a new model family: the open model ecosystem moves fast, and the candidate usually looks great in evals or promises better throughput. You want it in front of every user without hiccups, and a way to rollback if it disappoints. The usual options force a tradeoff: Both of these options put a human in the loop as the safety mechanism. Rollouts move that mechanism into the platform: you describe the source, the target, the steps, and what "healthy" means, and the platform works against this plan at every stage. A rollout migrates traffic between two deployments on the same endpoint: a source (what's serving today) and a target (what you want to serve tomorrow). Public benchmarks provide common reference points for tracking progress and comparing models, but they are not a good measure of real work. These evals use bounded tasks, fixed datasets, and standardized scoring. Real work is messier. It involves incomplete information, changing scope, business constraints, complex judgment calls, multi-step workflows, and collaboration. This distinction matters for organizations seeking to determine if a model is good enough to automate human tasks. posts.excerpt: Sections: The unit of research is no longer the paper | Open Source Week | Why the pessimism is wrong | Let go of how you work. Not who you are. | What will research look like, and how do you train for it? | The renaissance is in academia In one of my classes I asked the question I was afraid to ask but I just needed the answer to: “Who is afraid of not getting a job after graduating?” About eighty percent of the 150 people in the room raised their hands. That is roughly 120 students answering, in one motion, that they do not believe there is a place for them in the future. The other story arrives by email. PhD students who cannot wait to graduate, because they want to join a frontier lab and they have concluded that research in academia is meaningless. They are counting the years until they can leave. I believe both stories are wrong, and wrong for the same reason. They assume the future of research belongs to whoever has the most GPUs. I think the opposite is true. Academia is probably about to have a renaissance, and the most exciting work of the next decade will happen in university labs — not in spite of their limited resources, but because of them. This week is our argument for that claim, and we are making it in code rather than in prose. This post has six parts: why a lab like ours now publishes ecosystems instead of papers; what is actually in this open-source week; why the pessimism I keep running into is mistaken; what to let go of, and what to hold on to; what research will look like once you have let go of it; and why the renaissance happens in academia…

posts.title: The frontier isn’t a model. It’s a router.
posts.summary: An oracle router over 18 models scores 97.6% on DeepSWE at $1.88 a task, vs. 74.1% for the best single model. See how FireRouter picks per task.
posts.excerpt: Sections: How much capability is already in the model pool? | You rarely need the most expensive model | A few models go a long way | The hard part is predicting which model to use | How Nexus Auto does it How much better could a coding agent perform if it used the best model for each task? The best single model, GPT-6 Astra, gets 74.1% of DeepSWE tasks at $6.52 each. Pick the right model for each task and the same eighteen models get 97.6% at $1.88. 23 points better, at under a third of the cost. That number comes from hindsight. We ran all eighteen models on every task first and picked the winner for each one. What it measures is the capability already sitting in the pool, but it’s split across models that nobody uses together. Putting them together is a router’s job. It picks which model handles each task before the work starts, and before is the hard part. Looking back, it’s easy to point at a task and name the model that would have done it better. A router has to choose before it sees the outcome, and a wrong choice costs far more than the few dollars it saved. We analyzed DeepSWE v1.1 , an agentic coding benchmark where the unit of work is an engineering task: the agent has to understand an issue, inspect a repository, use tools, edit code, execute it, and get the task to pass. The policy is deliberately simple. Pick one model at the start of a task and keep it for the whole run, with no switching mid-session. posts.title: Accelerating Long-Context and Agentic Inference with NVFP4 KV Cache
posts.summary: The KV cache is a fundamental building block of the modern LLM inference system. The context from multiple conversation rounds in agent sessions is cached as keys and values (KV) in GPU memory, allowing the model to reuse them during subsequent decoding steps.
posts.excerpt: Sections: NVFP4 KV Implementation in SGLang | NVFP4 KV Decode Attention Kernel Implementation | Experiments and Results | Accuracy | Performance | Decode Performance | Prefill Performance | Agentic Workloads The KV cache is a fundamental building block of the modern LLM inference system. The context from multiple conversation rounds in agent sessions is cached as keys and values (KV) in GPU memory, allowing the model to reuse them during subsequent decoding steps. When generating each new token, the new query token attends to the relevant past KV tokens from the KV cache. As context windows grow, storing and reading KV cache puts increasing pressure on GPU memory capacity and bandwidth. There are two complementary ways to address this pressure: expand the storage available to the cache, or reduce the amount of data stored per token. GPU memory provides fast access to active KV data, but its capacity is limited. A serving system handling many users or long-running sessions cannot keep every session’s cache resident indefinitely. Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache) extends the cache hierarchy into host memory and distributed storage, allowing the system to retain more context beyond the GPU. KV cache quantization addresses the other side of the problem. Storing K/V values in FP8 instead of BF16 roughly halves the data footprint and reduces the bytes read during decoding. This can improve performance when KV reads are a bandwidth bottleneck. The tradeoff is numerical precision: lower-bit representations introduce quantization error, and that error must remain small enough to…

posts.excerpt: At a high level, an agentic workload is characterized by four elements: Multi-turn: a session includes tens or hundreds of interactions between the user and assistant, compared with a handful in a chatbot scenario. These workloads combine long contexts and high prefill reuse with sub-agent bursts and numerous tool calls. Long context: system prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns make context accumulate quickly. High prefix reuse: since the conversation progresses linearly, where output from turn n-1 is concatenated to turn n (typically), most context can be served from KV cache rather than recomputed (this depends on the amount of storage available to store KV tensors). As n grows, the ratio of cached input relative to uncached typically tends towards 1. Sub-agent bursts: a session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, which create bursty KV-cache patterns. Read more about the methodology in our AgentX article. Performance per total cost of ownership (TCO) is one of the most important angles in which to evaluate AI accelerator performance. In the charts below, the Y-axis is total tokens per $1 TCO. Layers 1 and 14 retrieve rows keyed by hashed token n-grams from two large fp8 tables and gate the selected rows into the residual stream. posts.title: Tiered KV Cache Offloading in vLLM
posts.summary: A host-centric framework for scaling KV cache across host memory, filesystems, object stores, and remote peers — reducing recomputation and increasing serving capacity.
posts.excerpt: Sections: The Host-Centric Design | Fast accelerator release, just-in-time allocation | Consolidated I/O | Canonical memory layout | Simple secondary tiers | How Offloading and Reloading Work | Offload path | Reload path Long-context models and multi-turn conversations generate massive KV caches. When accelerator memory (e.g., GPU HBM) fills up, previously computed KV data is evicted. On the next request that needs it, vLLM must recompute it from scratch. Tiered KV cache offloading preserves evicted KV data across host memory, storage, and remote peers. Instead of recomputing, vLLM reloads the data from a lower tier — saving compute, reducing latency, and increasing the effective serving capacity of the cluster. With secondary tiers, KV data also becomes shareable across nodes — enabling horizontal scaling of the cache, warm-starting new instances from shared storage, and transferring KV data between peers for disaggregated serving or load balancing. The framework has been available in vLLM since v0.22 and a detailed usage guide can be found here . The core design principle: all KV data flows through host memory (CPU DRAM) . When offloading, KV data moves from accelerator to host first. From the host, it propagates to secondary tiers — filesystem, object storage, or remote peers. When reloading, the flow reverses: a secondary tier promotes data into host memory, then it is loaded to the accelerator. Copying from accelerator to host is a fast local PCIe transfer. Accelerator memory is freed as soon as this copy completes — before any secondary tier transfer starts. Storage…

Each of those is a shuffle. Shuffle is the one operation Ray Data cannot stream. A map or a write takes a block, transforms it, and passes it downstream, so peak memory tracks block size rather than dataset size. groupby, join, and repartition require every row sharing a key to be gathered in one place, so a shuffle worker holds a partition, and partition size is the dataset divided by the partition count. Ten times the data means ten times the memory in that worker. Shuffle is where these pipelines fail, where the OOMs happen, and where a job that ran fine at 100 GB falls over at 1 TB. Shuffle V2 is a redesign of Ray Data's shuffle engine. It materializes shuffle intermediates in the object store instead of accumulating them in a long-lived aggregator, which gives us: Stability: shards live in the object store, spilled to disk when it fills, so intermediates no longer pile up in a worker's heap. In our experiments, its effect on output-token throughput varied across drafting methods and proposal lengths, and also depended on the model family, draft checkpoint, workload, and acceptance behavior. Large language models support a wide range of applications, but serving them at scale requires careful optimization. Standard autoregressive decoding is the baseline used by most LLM serving systems: the model generates one token, appends it to the sequence, and then uses the updated sequence to generate the next token. This process is simple and reliable, but the serving loop still advances one committed token at a time because output tokens must be produced in strict left-to-right order. Speculative decoding [1] builds on this baseline through a draft-and-verify mechanism. A lightweight draft component proposes candidate future tokens, and the target model verifies those candidates before they are committed. When several draft tokens are accepted, the system can commit multiple output tokens from a single target-model verification step while preserving the target model's output behavior. In serving ML models, some applications make a single model call that runs for several seconds to minutes, e.g. - transcribing an hour of audio, indexing a video, or generating an image or a video. On a normal synchronous HTTP endpoint the request stays open for the whole computation. At millisecond latencies that coupling is invisible, but for calls this long it creates two problems. First, a burst of traffic piles onto a fleet that takes seconds or minutes to finish each request, so the workers fall behind and clients, or any intermediary hop, start timing out. Also, a connection held open for minutes has much more exposure to a dropped packet or a failed hop. As a result, the service and overall system gets less reliable at exactly the moments you can't predict. posts.title: Unified Radix Cache: One Tree for Hybrid Model Prefix Caching
posts.summary: Prefix caching reuses KV when requests share the same token prefix. Under full attention, once the KV for a shared prefix is computed, it remains valid as more tokens are appended. A later request with the same prefix can reuse those KV entries instead of recomputing them during prefill.
posts.excerpt: Sections: Introduction | Highlights | One Tree, Composable Components | Finding a Safe Reuse Boundary | Component Hooks Across the Tree Lifecycle | Native HiCache Across Memory Tiers | Components, Anchors, and Sidecars | HiCache Multi-Turn Benchmark Results Prefix caching reuses KV when requests share the same token prefix. Under full attention, once the KV for a shared prefix is computed, it remains valid as more tokens are appended. A later request with the same prefix can reuse those KV entries instead of recomputing them during prefill. SGLang tracks this mapping with a radix tree keyed by token sequences. Before prefill, the tree finds the longest reusable prefix and returns its KV locations to the scheduler. Hybrid models break this single reuse rule. A request may combine full attention KV, sliding window attention KV, and recurrent states, each with a different notion of reuse. Full attention KV remains reusable across the entire matched prefix. Sliding window attention KV covers only the trailing window. A recurrent state is valid only at an exact prefix checkpoint. They share the same token prefix, but not the same reusable boundary . Forcing a single boundary across all of them either discards valid reuse or permits invalid reuse. These reuse rules appear in different combinations across model families. Encoding each combination as a specialized cache class creates a combinatorial class matrix, especially once orthogonal capabilities such as HiCache are added. Earlier implementations followed this pattern, duplicating matching, insertion, locking, and eviction…

This post explains the architectural changes proposed in SGLang issue #15194 . The new design separates checkpoint interpretation, parameter registration, weight loading, post-processing, and kernel execution into focused, reusable components. Production serving engines can no longer rely on a single low-bit kernel. They must handle diverse checkpoint formats such as AWQ, GPTQ, Compressed-Tensors, ModelSlim, and Quark; dense and MoE weights; KV cache formats; attention kernels; and hardware-specific execution across CUDA GPUs, Ascend NPUs, CPUs, and other backends. When format parsing, parameter registration, weight loading, post-processing, platform checks, and kernel execution are all placed in one class, each new format or backend increases coupling. The result becomes harder to review, test, reuse, and extend. In the old design, a single quantization method often owned the entire path: defining parameters, loading weights, transforming layouts, selecting a backend, and launching the kernel. Supporting another platform meant adding more branches to the same format-facing class, even when much of the hardware logic could have been reused…

posts.title: A note on the Hugging Face agent incident
posts.summary: Hugging Face published a technical timeline of a recent agent intrusion. Modal's platform and isolation were not compromised in this incident.
posts.excerpt: Hugging Face published a technical timeline of a recent agent intrusion, which names Modal as the third-party infrastructure the agent used as a launchpad. Modal's platform and isolation were not compromised in any way. The environment involved was a customer's own application. It was deployed to a endpoint that was publicly accessible without authentication, and it was designed to compile and execute code submitted by anyone on the internet in a Modal Sandbox. The code execution the attacker obtained took place inside that customer's own container, within Modal's standard sandbox isolation boundary. No other customer workloads were affected. While customers can expose Sandboxes to unauthenticated traffic, this is never the default, and Modal provides the authentication, network, and monitoring controls to keep production workloads locked down. We recommend that anything exposed to the public internet require authentication , IP allowlist, restrict its outbound network access to only what it needs, and treat any code or input it accepts from users as untrusted. For additional questions, email security@modal.com .

OPD is now integrated into Miles rollout and training flow, so users can train a student model either solely with a teacher model’s guidance, or combine teacher guidance with GRPO/PPO-style reinforcement learning objectives. The experiment shows that without any task-specific reward, OPD can transfer a teacher model’s shorter-reasoning behavior to a base student model while preserving the student model’s performance. Miles now supports OPD as an additive reverse-KL training signal. This enables OPD to support two important modes. On the rollout side, Miles supports both sampled-token OPD and top-k OPD through an SGLang-hosted teacher. In sampled-token OPD, the teacher scores the token actually sampled by the student at each response position. Because sampling may be stochastic, this token is not necessarily the student’s highest-probability token. Top-k OPD extends this workflow by retaining multiple candidate tokens and their student logprobs at each position. The teacher scores those same…

posts.title: What does 99.9% uptime mean for inference?
posts.summary: Reliability numbers are easy to publish. We break down what 99%, 99.9%, and 99.99% uptime actually require, the failure domains each tier has to survive, and the questions to ask any inference provider before you commit.
posts.excerpt: Sections: The problem with reliability numbers | What each nine actually requires | 99%: Survive node failures | 99.9%: Survive a full DC failure | 99.99%: Survive a regional outage | What to ask before you commit to a provider | Our numbers defined | Come see the architecture Reliability numbers are easy to publish. What’s hard is explaining what they mean: which failure domains the architecture actually covers, whether the provider controls the infrastructure at those layers, and what happens when something breaks at 3 a.m. Together runs inference for teams like Cursor, Decagon, Cartesia, and Yutori. We’ve been paged for most of what follows; here’s what we’ve learned. When inference goes down, someone’s product goes down with it. GPU inference fails differently from conventional services. The hardware has failure modes; CPU infrastructure doesn't, and the systems are tuned hard for performance. Hitting 1M tokens per minute per GPU at 200 TPS, or sub-50ms TTFT on voice models with custom kernels, leaves limited slack. Adding reliability to a system like that is exponentially harder with each nine. The useful mental model is layers, and the failure modes in each one are distinct: None of these fail in isolation. A storage hiccup surfaces as a capacity problem, a thermal event shows up as degraded output quality long before any health alert fires. Getting good at this means learning to read the real signal from the misleading symptom. Each tier is a different engineering problem, not just a harder version of the same one. Here’s what each one actually takes, and what we’ve…

Misha's focus areas are unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. In our last posts we introduced reinforcement learning (RL) intuitively , explained why it’s important, and defined a general mathematical framework for building RL agents . As a recap, we defined the goal of RL algorithms in the following way: 💡 The goal of an RL algorithm is to learn a policy that achieves the maximum expected returns in its environment. We know that RL algorithms should maximize expected returns, but what objective should they optimize? For a common machine learning problem like regression, we might optimize the model by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE). A neural network that minimizes the MSE will become better at predicting continuous valued targets given some input data. Can we find a similar notion of “error” that when minimized will result in the agent maximizing rewards? Yes — and to do so we’ll introduce Q functions. A Q function is just another name for the expected returns and the agent’s goal is to achieve . Q functions are also known as action-value functions because they predict how much return an agent expects to get if it takes a specific action.
